children: As rental transactions move onto digital platforms, unresolved deposit settlements and weak documentation continue to challenge tenant-landlord relationships across metros

India’s rental housing market is grappling with a set of operational gaps that extend beyond monthly rent, from high security deposits and disputed deductions to delayed refunds and scattered records. As digital payments evolve towards AI-led and agentic transactions, these gaps are bringing greater focus on how technology could reshape routine rental processes.

Nearly Rs 1.26 lakh crore in security deposits is estimated to be locked with landlords across six major metros, underscoring the scale of the settlement problem. Industry stakeholders say AI could automate payment tracking, documentation, deductions and refunds, but the larger challenge remains creating a standardised and trusted system that both tenants and landlords can rely on.

Security-deposit settlement remains one of the least standardised stages of rental transactions. Deposits in Indian metros can range between two and 10 months’ rent, while the Model Tenancy Act proposes a two-month cap for residential leases, according to Savills India.

Saurabh Bhutani, Senior Director, Research & Consulting, Savills India, said, “The biggest inefficiency in rental transactions is the lack of transparency and standardisation during security-deposit settlement. In Indian metros, deposits can range from 2–10 months’ rent.”

Deductions for repairs, cleaning, maintenance and utilities are often assessed manually, contributing to disputes and delayed refunds. Bhutani said, “AI can create a digital audit trail by analysing move-in/move-out images, validating invoices, tracking payments, calculating deductions, and automating reconciliation and refunds.”
Rental Records Lack Standardisation

The deposit issue is also linked to the absence of a common record showing what landlords and tenants agreed to, what has been paid and what remains payable. This leaves reconciliation dependent on fragmented documentation and manual intervention.

Dr. Amit Goenka, Chairman & MD, Nisus Finance, said, “The immediate opportunity I would see is in bringing greater discipline to the whole of the rental transaction. Rent collection is only part of the equation. Tracking deposits, reconciling payments and documenting deductions are just as important.”

Goenka said the problem extends to establishing accountability around settlement. “To me, the biggest inefficiency is not having a common, trusted record of what both sides have agreed and what is still payable. AI is able to help connect those records, and spot discrepancies early.”
Agencies Face Operational Shift

Rental agencies and property managers handle several repetitive functions, including payment reminders, documentation, tenant follow-ups and receipt verification. AI could reduce the administrative workload associated with these activities, although more complex interactions would continue to require human intervention.

Rupam Dey, Head - Marketing Communication & Brand, Hubtown, said, “The use of AI technology can make the work of property management agencies less time consuming by doing reminders, documentations, payment tracking and communicating. This will help in saving money and time for the agency.”

The change could alter the nature of intermediary work rather than eliminate it. Dey said, “There is going to be a need for human intervention in areas such as negotiation, inspection, dispute resolution and decision making. This means that the role of agencies is likely to change from one of transactional work to added value services provision.”
AI Meets Infrastructure Gaps

Bengaluru’s rental market illustrates the underlying challenge, with 75 per cent of tenants citing high security deposits as a barrier, while only 35 per cent received their last security deposit in full, according to industry report.. The figures point to settlement and trust issues that extend beyond the payment mechanism.

The technology could make records easier to verify, but Bhutani sees the wider rental framework as equally important. “By integrating lease agreements, payment records, inspection reports and maintenance logs into a single digital workflow, AI can create a verifiable audit trail and significantly reduce disputes.”

That framework would also determine how much confidence tenants and landlords can place in an AI-assisted settlement. Dey said, “Renting could become significantly more transparent and efficient through the use of AI technology. Currently, there is a lot of manual labor involved in rent collection, deposit processing, documentation and refunds which results in a large number of mistakes and discrepancies.”
Trust Could Shape Adoption

Agentic payments introduce another layer to rental transactions by allowing AI systems to execute payments based on predefined instructions. For a market involving recurring rent and substantial security deposits, adoption would depend on whether users are willing to delegate controlled financial functions to AI.

Goenka said the process should begin with limited, pre-authorised instructions rather than wider financial authority. “Users would need to be able to immediately withdraw permission, receive transaction alerts, access records, and place limits on payments. Changes in rent, other charges and disputed deductions should require explicit approval.”

The emphasis on control reflects the broader challenge of introducing AI into financial transactions involving landlords and tenants. “If an agent makes a mistake, it is necessary to specify the issue of responsibility. Users will need to be in control and have effective recourse for trust to be,” Goenka said.
